1. Metastatic follicular (differentiated) thyroid carcinoma to the manubrium — biopsy shows thyroid follicular cells infiltrating bone; FTC classically spreads hematogenously to bone and fits the clinical/imaging pattern.
2. Metastatic follicular-variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (FVPTC) — a differentiated thyroid cancer with follicular architecture that can behave like FTC and produce osseous metastases; histology can overlap.
3. Metastasis from an occult thyroid primary arising in residual right thyroid lobe (iodine-avid differentiated thyroid carcinoma) — prior left hemithyroidectomy leaves residual thyroid as a plausible primary site.
4. Tissue contamination or needle-track seeding with benign thyroid tissue (artifact) superimposed on a primary sternal neoplasm (e.g., chondrosarcoma) — unlikely because histology shows true invasion of bone trabeculae rather than isolated thyroid fragments, but must be considered if clinical correlation/primary thyroid imaging disproves a malignant thyroid source.
5. Primary sternal infection/osteomyelitis or chronic abscess with entrapped thyroid tissue — least likely given negative cultures and the presence of organized thyroid follicles infiltrating bone rather than inflammatory granulation tissue.

If you would like, next steps I recommend (not requested now as part of this answer) are serum thyroglobulin with anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, TSH, high-resolution ultrasound of the remaining thyroid, and whole-body radioiodine scanning (or FDG-PET if non-iodine-avid) for staging and to localize the primary and additional metastases.
